summary: Describes an architecture for service assurance in intent-based networking. It decomposes a service into subservices and uses a holistic view of network devices and functions to correlate service degradation with symptoms in specific components.

plainLanguage.summary: To know whether a big machine works, check each part and see which part is the cause of any trouble.

questions: how to find which component degrades a service
how does service assurance for intent based networking work
what is a health score in sain
subtitle: How to break a network service into parts, watch each part, and say which one is making the service sick.

tldr.problem: Knowing that a service configuration was applied does not show that the service is actually working, and operators struggle to link a degraded service to a failing network component, or the reverse.
tldr.mechanism: The SAIN architecture turns a service instance into an assurance graph of subservices and dependencies, has agents compute a health score from 0 to 100 plus symptoms for each node, and has a collector gather the results.
tldr.outcome: Operators can see which subservice likely explains a degraded service and which services are affected by a failing component. The interfaces are defined as YANG modules in a companion document, RFC 9418.

today: RFC 9417 is an Informational RFC from July 2023, and its metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFCs. The YANG modules that implement the architecture are defined in the companion RFC 9418.

sections.title: Why Service Assurance
sections.content:
A service orchestrator can push a configuration to many devices, but a configuration being applied does not mean the service is up and running as expected. The service may be degraded by a network failure, or a service function may answer at the IP level without doing its job. Operators therefore need to monitor operational data together with configuration, and model-driven telemetry reuses the same YANG data models for both.

Even so, it is hard to answer questions such as why an L3VPN fails to connect, or which services are hurt when an optic starts to degrade. This RFC defines an architecture for Service Assurance for Intent-based Networking (SAIN). Instead of requiring a declared intent, it infers what the service working as expected means from the configuration pushed to the devices, and uses the service model for the intent when one is available.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling a computer to do something is not the same as checking that it happened. SAIN is the checking part.

sections.title: Assurance Graphs and Subservices
sections.content:
A service instance is decomposed into subservices, each a part of the network that can be assured on its own. The result is an assurance graph, a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose nodes are the service instance and its subservices and whose edges are dependencies. In the RFC's example, a tunnel service depends on two tunnel interfaces and on IP connectivity, which depends on the IS-IS routing protocol. The tunnel interfaces depend on physical interfaces, which depend on devices.

Decomposition lets experts own their part, for example an optics expert for the optic subservice, and lets shared subservices be reused. A subservice is identified by a minimal set of parameters, such as a device ID, that cannot change during its life. An IP address is a poor parameter for identifying an interface, since the address can change.

Combining graphs from different designers can create circular dependencies. The RFC suggests detecting them in the SAIN orchestrator and, as a more elaborate fix, replacing each strongly connected component with a synthetic node that depends on every member.
sections.plainLanguage: A big toy is built from smaller parts, and each part sits on top of others. If the bottom part breaks, everything resting on it is in trouble.

sections.title: The Functional Architecture
sections.content:
The SAIN orchestrator takes the service configuration and builds the assurance graph. It sends the graph to SAIN agents, which fetch metrics from devices, build the expression graph and compute health statuses in a distributed way. The SAIN collector receives the output, displays it, detects changes in the graph structure (such as a switchover from primary to backup path) and passes them back to the orchestrator. Feedback to the service orchestrator closes the automation loop.

The components can be combined or distributed. The service and SAIN orchestrators are likely combined in practice, and an agent can run inside the device it monitors. Different agents may handle different subgraphs, for example one per peer, and the collector stitches them together. The notion of service is generic: it can cover a DHCP server, a routing instance or a service function in a chain.

Time synchronization between all elements is required, with NTP as a candidate, so that symptoms line up with the right version of the assurance graph.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper draws the map of parts, little inspectors check each part, and a manager gathers their reports and says what is wrong.

sections.title: Health Scores, Symptoms and Dependencies
sections.content:
For every service instance and subservice, SAIN computes a health score, an integer from 0 to 100, where 0 means broken and 100 means operating as expected. The special value -1 means no value could be computed, for example because a metric was missing. Any score below the maximum must be explained by one or more symptoms, such as "Interface has high error rate". Score plus symptoms is the health status. The exact meaning of score values is out of scope.

The assurance graph is turned into an expression graph that says which metrics to fetch and how to compute each status. Combining depends on the dependency type. An impacting dependency affects the parent's score and its symptoms count as reasons, while an informational dependency does not affect the score, though its symptoms are shown. More types may be defined by extending the YANG module.

Subservices must not depend on how a metric is collected. A metric engine inside the agent maps each device-independent metric to device-specific implementations, such as a standard YANG model, a vendor model, a MIB module or the CLI.
sections.plainLanguage: Every part gets a mark out of 100 and a note saying why it lost points. Some parts really change the grade of the thing above them, and some are only extra notes.

sections.title: Maintenance Windows and Graph Changes
sections.content:
During maintenance an operator wants to silence expected symptoms. The YANG model lets a subservice be flagged as under maintenance, with a string naming the person or process that requested it. That subservice reports only a generic "Under Maintenance" symptom, and any other symptom from it or its impacting dependencies must not be reported. In the RFC's tunnel example, flagging the Peer1 device silences everything but "Under Maintenance" on its interfaces and the tunnel service instance, and leaves other subservices unaffected.

Where a subservice only partly impacts a service, for instance a primary path under maintenance with a working backup, the service may show symptoms such as "No redundancy". Unflagging maintenance should trigger an assurance graph update.

The graph changes over time, so an assurance graph version and last-change time are kept. A collector that sees a change processes only subservice instances whose last change is newer than the time it remembered. Symptoms have start and end dates, and an agent may drop old ones, so a history start date tells the collector what the agent still reports.
sections.plainLanguage: If a machine is being fixed on purpose, you mute its alarms and only say "being fixed", so nobody panics.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SAIN agents must be secured, since a compromised agent could send incorrect root causes or symptoms to management systems. Protecting them comes down to the integrity and confidentiality of the assurance graph, partly by setting permissions on YANG nodes as described in RFC 9418. Apart from telemetry configuration, agents need no write access to the devices they monitor, and should have their own credentials limited to those nodes.

The collected data may reveal how the network is designed, so data access concerns should be weighed against the value of quick root-cause finding. In a closed-loop system, a lying device or compromised agent could trigger partial reconfiguration, a risk SAIN neither adds to nor removes. If NTP fails, clocks drift and correlating symptoms across devices becomes inaccurate.
sections.plainLanguage: Inspectors must be honest and locked in with the right keys. If one lies, the manager gets a wrong story.

items.title: SAIN orchestrator
items.text: Fetches service configuration and converts it into an assurance graph.

items.title: SAIN agent
items.text: Builds the expression graph, fetches metrics and computes health status, possibly on the monitored device.

items.title: SAIN collector
items.text: Gathers and displays health status and reports graph changes back to the orchestrator.

items.title: Metric engine
items.text: Part of the agent; maps device-independent metrics to device-specific implementations.

cells: Does not change the parent's score
